alertRuleForm_description: A saved condition plus a count threshold, evaluated on a rolling window every poll interval.
alertRuleForm_anomalyBaselineLabel: Compared with the same window on each of the previous
alertRuleForm_anomalyHint: Fires when the current value is further from its usual level at this time of day (or week) than the z-score allows. At least 3 of the previous periods need data before it can fire. 3 is sensitive; 4-5 is quieter.
alertRuleForm_anomalyWindowTooLong: The window must be shorter than one baseline period (1 day for days, 1 week for weeks).
alertRuleForm_exceptionMessageHint: Leave empty to match every message for this exception type.
alertRuleForm_gaugeMatchHintGreaterOrEqu: Value = window average · Last = latest point · Min = breached the whole window · Max = breached at least once
alertRuleForm_gaugeMatchHintLessThan: Value = window average · Last = latest point · Min = breached at least once · Max = breached the whole window
alertRuleForm_cooldownHint: Minimum time between two notifications, even if it keeps breaching.
alertRuleForm_noDataLabel: Also alert when there is no data
alertRuleForm_noDataHint: Fires if the condition matches nothing at all over this window, like a stopped exporter or a service that went silent. Minimum {min} seconds.
alertRuleForm_minDataPointsLabel: Require a minimum number of data points
alertRuleForm_minDataPointsHint: With fewer points than this in the window, the rule reports insufficient data and doesn't fire, so an average over one or two sparse samples can't trigger it. Counts raw points across every matched series.
alertRuleForm_templateTitleHint: Used as the email subject and PagerDuty summary, and as the first line on other channels. Leave empty to keep the built-in title.
alertRuleForm_templateBodyHint: Replaces the whole built-in message, links included, so add the rule_url / data_url placeholders where you want them. Leave empty to keep the built-in message.
alertRuleForm_templateLabelsHint: plus labels.<key> for the rule's service and attribute filters, e.g. labels.service.name.
alertRuleForm_evaluateEveryHint: How often this rule is checked. Pick a longer interval for slow or expensive rules. It can't be longer than the window.
alertRuleForm_evaluateEveryTooLong: The interval is longer than the window, so part of every interval would never be checked. Shorten the interval or widen the window.

indexingTablesTable_partsExplanation1: ClickHouse stores each table's data in immutable parts and periodically merges them together in the background.
indexingTablesTable_partsExplanation2: A high active-part count means merges aren't keeping up - it slows queries (every part is a separate read) and usually points to small, frequent inserts rather than fewer, larger ones. Flare flags {threshold}+ active parts as high fragmentation - the same point at which ClickHouse itself starts throttling inserts to let merges catch up.

authToggleCard_description: Off by default - anyone who can reach this dashboard has full access. Turn this on to require signing in, then enable and configure at least one method below.

entraSecurityForm_description: Before Flare can authenticate users against your Entra ID directory, it must be registered as an {app} in that directory. Create an App Registration in the Azure portal and paste the resulting values below - see docs/auth.md for the full walkthrough. Each self-hosted Flare instance uses its own App Registration; nothing here is shared across deployments.
entraSecurityForm_savedRestart: Saved. Restart Flare.Api for this to take effect.
entraSecurityForm_redirectUriHint: You must configure this {exact} redirect URI (reply URL) in your Entra ID app registration.
entraSecurityForm_clientSecretHint: Client secret assigned to the Flare application. Leave blank to keep the currently-saved value - it is never displayed once set.
ldapSecurityForm_description: Point Flare at your Active Directory (or AD-compatible) directory over LDAP/LDAPS. Flare binds once with the service account below to find a submitted username's real DN, then re-binds as that DN with the submitted password to verify it - see docs/auth.md for the full walkthrough.
ldapSecurityForm_pinnedCertHint: Paste your internal CA's root certificate, or the domain controller's own certificate if it's self-signed. You can paste more than one certificate back to back (e.g. a root {and} the intermediate that actually signed the DC's certificate, or two DC certificates to ride out a rotation) - same concatenated-PEM convention as any CA bundle file. When set, Flare trusts {only} the certificate(s) pasted here for LDAP connections, bypassing the host's OS trust store. Leave blank to use the OS trust store (default). Get this with, e.g. {cmd} - its output already includes the full chain.
ldapSecurityForm_bindPasswordHint: Leave blank to keep the currently-saved value - it is never displayed once set.
ldapSecurityForm_defaultRoleHint: Assigned on first sign-in when someone isn't a member of any of the three group DNs above.
ldapSecurityForm_userFilterHint: {placeholder} is replaced with the submitted username (escaped).
ldapSecurityForm_uniqueIdHint: AD's stable per-account identifier - {code} by default.
oidcSecurityForm_description: Sign in against any standards-compliant OpenID Connect provider - Okta, Auth0, Keycloak, Authentik, and the like. Register Flare as an application with your provider first, then paste the resulting values below - see docs/auth.md for the full walkthrough.
oidcSecurityForm_savedRestart: Saved. Restart Flare.Api for this to take effect.
oidcSecurityForm_callbackUrlHint: You must configure this {exact} callback (redirect) URL in your OpenID Connect provider.
oidcSecurityForm_displayNameHint: Shown on the sign-in page as "Sign in with {name}".
oidcSecurityForm_authorityHint: The URL of the OpenID Connect authorization server.
oidcSecurityForm_scopesHint: Scopes Flare will request when authenticating users, separated by spaces.
oidcSecurityForm_roleClaimHint: The token claim carrying {roleCodes} - unlike Entra ID's fixed {rolesClaim} claim, generic providers vary in what they issue.
oidcSecurityForm_defaultRoleHint: Assigned on first sign-in when the role claim above is absent or unrecognized.
proxyAuthSecurityForm_description: Trust an identity header from a reverse proxy that already authenticates requests in front of Flare (Authelia, Authentik, oauth2-proxy, Cloudflare Access, Tailscale Serve, ...) - no separate sign-in flow, Flare just reads the header. See docs/auth.md for the full walkthrough and the security model.
proxyAuthSecurityForm_headerNameHint: The request header the proxy sets to the signed-in user's identity.
proxyAuthSecurityForm_trustedCidrsHint: One or more CIDR ranges, one per line - {required} to enable this method. The header above is only trusted from a caller whose own address falls inside one of these ranges, since the header itself can be spoofed by anyone who can reach Flare.Api directly.
proxyAuthSecurityForm_groupsHeaderHint: A second header carrying comma-separated group names. Leave blank to always assign Default role below.
proxyAuthSecurityForm_logoutRedirectHint: Flare can't log a user out of the proxy's own session - it only clears Flare's own cookie. Left blank, clicking "Log out" just returns to /login, which signs back in silently as long as the proxy keeps sending the header. Set this to your proxy's own sign-out URL (or the identity provider's) to send the browser there instead.
proxyAuthSecurityForm_defaultRoleHint: Assigned on first sign-in when no groups header is configured, or its value matches none of the three groups above.
userTable_description: Manage accounts and roles - local, Microsoft Entra ID, and Active Directory alike.
dataSourcesPage_description: Flare.Ingest speaks plain OTLP (and can pull Prometheus metrics directly) - pick where your data is coming from for a ready-to-run snippet.
dataSourceCatalog_kubernetesIntro: Run the OpenTelemetry Collector as a DaemonSet so it tails every pod's container logs and forwards them to Flare.Ingest over OTLP.
dataSourceCatalog_kubernetesStep2Body: Replace the endpoint below with wherever Flare.Ingest is reachable from inside the cluster - a Service DNS name if it runs in-cluster too, an external host:port otherwise.
dataSourceCatalog_dockerIntro: Already have an OTLP exporter in your app? Point it at Flare.Ingest with standard OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_* environment variables - no collector needed in between.
dataSourceCatalog_dockerStep1Body: "ingest" is the service name Flare's own docker-compose.yml gives Flare.Ingest - use whatever name your Flare.Ingest container has, as long as both containers share a network.
dataSourceCatalog_dockerStep2Body: Same variables work for a container (or any process) outside the compose network - point at the published host ports instead.
dataSourceCatalog_linuxIntro: Run the OpenTelemetry Collector to tail log files (or receive OTLP from local apps) and forward everything to Flare.
dataSourceCatalog_linuxStep3Body: Wrap this in a systemd unit for anything beyond a quick test.
dataSourceCatalog_windowsIntro: Run the OpenTelemetry Collector as a local OTLP relay, or skip it entirely and point an app's own exporter straight at Flare (see Languages & Frameworks) - same protocol either way.
dataSourceCatalog_windowsStep1Body: Grab otelcol-contrib_windows_amd64.tar.gz from the OpenTelemetry Collector releases page.
dataSourceCatalog_windowsStep2Body: Receives OTLP from apps on this machine and forwards to Flare - add the contrib windowseventlog receiver alongside otlp if you also want the Windows Event Log.
dataSourceCatalog_dotnetIntro: The standard OpenTelemetry .NET SDK exports logs straight to Flare - no Flare-specific package required.
dataSourceCatalog_dotnetStep3Body: Flare ships an Aspire.Flare package that does the above for you, reading the endpoint from a connection string (e.g. .WithReference(flare) on the AppHost side) instead of a hardcoded URI.
dataSourceCatalog_pythonIntro: Zero-code instrumentation - wrap your app's start command, no source changes needed.
dataSourceCatalog_nodejsIntro: Zero-code instrumentation via the auto-instrumentations meta-package.
dataSourceCatalog_javaIntro: Zero-code instrumentation via the OpenTelemetry Java agent - attach it and set environment variables, no source changes.
dataSourceCatalog_javaStep2Heading: Run your app with it attached
dataSourceCatalog_goIntro: Go has no zero-code agent for logs yet - wire the SDK's OTLP log exporter directly.
dataSourceCatalog_goStep2Body: The Go logs SDK is newer than traces/metrics and its API has moved faster between releases - check go.opentelemetry.io/otel's own docs if this doesn't match your installed version.
dataSourceCatalog_jenkinsIntro: Jenkins doesn't speak OTLP itself - which approach fits depends on how it's deployed.
dataSourceCatalog_jenkinsStep1Body: Nothing Jenkins-specific needed - the Kubernetes/Docker items on the Platforms tab already tail container stdout/stderr and forward it as OTLP.
dataSourceCatalog_jenkinsStep2Heading: Running on a VM or bare metal?
dataSourceCatalog_jenkinsStep2Body: Same idea as the Platforms tab's Linux/Windows items - point the Collector's filelog receiver at Jenkins' own log file instead of /var/log/**/*.log (the default location varies by install: a .deb/.rpm package writes to /var/log/jenkins/jenkins.log; running the .war directly just logs to stdout, so tail wherever that's redirected to).
dataSourceCatalog_jenkinsStep3Heading: Want per-build traces instead of raw log lines?
dataSourceCatalog_jenkinsStep3Body: Jenkins' official OpenTelemetry plugin exports each pipeline run as OTel traces (one span per stage/step) via OTLP directly - no Collector needed. It's built on the OTel Java SDK, so it reads the same standard environment variables; whether it also ships build console logs (not just traces) depends on your installed plugin version's own config screen (Manage Jenkins → Configure System → OpenTelemetry).
dataSourceCatalog_ansibleIntro: A playbook run is ephemeral, not a long-running service - the community.general collection ships an OpenTelemetry callback plugin that exports each run as an OTel trace (one span per task) instead.
dataSourceCatalog_ansibleStep2Heading: Enable the callback and point it at Flare
dataSourceCatalog_ansibleStep2Body: Double-check these env var names against your installed community.general version - callback plugin configuration has shifted across releases.
dataSourceCatalog_ansibleStep3Heading: Running via AWX/Tower, or just want the raw log?
dataSourceCatalog_ansibleStep3Body: Treat it like any other Linux service and tail its log file instead - see the Platforms tab.
dataSourceCatalog_terraformIntro: A terraform apply run is even more ephemeral than a playbook, and the CLI has no OTLP exporter of its own - get its debug log onto disk, then forward that.
dataSourceCatalog_terraformStep1Heading: Turn on Terraform's own debug log
dataSourceCatalog_terraformStep2Body: Tail terraform.log the same way the Platforms tab's Linux item tails any other log file - point the Collector's filelog receiver at it.
dataSourceCatalog_terraformStep3Heading: In ephemeral CI (e.g. a GitHub-hosted runner)
dataSourceCatalog_terraformStep3Body: There's no host left for a Collector to read from once the job ends - see the GitHub Actions item for shipping a run's outcome directly from the workflow instead.
dataSourceCatalog_githubActionsIntro: No native OTLP exporter for Actions - the reliable option is a workflow step that ships the job's outcome directly, the same shape as the Custom tab's raw curl example.
dataSourceCatalog_githubActionsStep1Body: Treat the runner like any other Linux/Windows host - see the Platforms tab. Nothing GitHub-specific needed.
dataSourceCatalog_githubActionsStep2Body: The runner disappears once the job ends, so add a step that reports the outcome directly instead, using GitHub's own workflow context. This is a minimal example (one log event per run) - free-text values like a commit message would need real JSON escaping (e.g. via jq) before going in the body.
dataSourceCatalog_vectorIntro: Vector ships a native OpenTelemetry sink - point it at Flare.Ingest directly, no separate Collector needed.
dataSourceCatalog_vectorStep1Body: inputs should list whatever source or transform is already producing the events you want shipped - a file source tailing a log, a docker_logs source, etc.
dataSourceCatalog_fluentBitIntro: Fluent Bit ships a built-in OpenTelemetry output plugin - point it at Flare.Ingest directly, no separate Collector needed.
dataSourceCatalog_syslogIntro: Flare.Ingest has no syslog listener of its own - route through the OpenTelemetry Collector's syslog receiver instead, same pattern as any other source that doesn't speak OTLP.
dataSourceCatalog_syslogStep1Body: Runs alongside whatever else the Collector is already doing on this host - see the Platforms tab for the full install steps (this is just the receiver/exporter pair to add to that config).
dataSourceCatalog_syslogStep2Body: Point whatever's emitting syslog (a network device, syslog-ng, journald's syslog forwarding, etc.) at this host on port 5514 instead of wherever it was going before.
dataSourceCatalog_prometheusIntro: The only pull-based source on this page - Flare.Ingest scrapes a Prometheus-style /metrics endpoint itself on a timer, instead of something exporting to Flare. No exporter, sidecar, or Collector needed on the target's side.
dataSourceCatalog_prometheusStep1Body: Add this to Flare.Ingest's configuration (appsettings.json, or an appsettings.Production.json override) and restart it - Job becomes the service.name every point from this target is tagged with, matching the OTel Collector's own prometheusreceiver convention.
dataSourceCatalog_prometheusStep2Body: Same shape, no file to mount - .NET's standard double-underscore config-key binding reaches the same array/object structure. "ingest" is Flare's own docker-compose.yml service name; the target itself just needs to be reachable from that container's network.
dataSourceCatalog_prometheusStep3Body: Headers are sent on every scrape request (e.g. a bearer token). Labels are merged onto every point's resource attributes, applied after - and able to override - the computed service.name/service.instance.id.
dataSourceCatalog_prometheusStep4Body: Give it one scrape interval, then look for the target's metric names on the Metrics page, or watch the "Prometheus scrape" row on the Ingestion page's Receivers table for real request counts.
dataSourceCatalog_kafkaIntro: Send your .NET producers' and consumers' Kafka spans to Flare, plus consumer lag from the OpenTelemetry Collector. Together they fill the Messaging page: publish and consume rates, errors, latency and lag per topic.
dataSourceCatalog_kafkaStep2Heading: Build clients with the instrumented builders
dataSourceCatalog_kafkaStep2Body: Pass the same builder instances to the tracer and use them to build your clients. Clients built with the plain Confluent builders emit no spans, and the builders need a ProducerConfig/ConsumerConfig object, not a plain key/value list.
dataSourceCatalog_kafkaStep3Body: Consumer lag isn't in spans. Run the OpenTelemetry Collector (contrib distribution) with the kafkametrics receiver pointed at your brokers. Collector 0.161 and later call it kafka_metrics; the old name still works.
dataSourceCatalog_kafkaStep4Body: Produce and consume a few messages, then open Messaging in the top nav. Each topic appears within a few seconds; lag appears after one collection interval.
dataSourceCatalog_rabbitmqIntro: Send your .NET publishers' and consumers' RabbitMQ spans to Flare, plus queue depth from the OpenTelemetry Collector. Together they fill the Messaging page: publish and consume rates, errors, latency and backlog per exchange or queue.
dataSourceCatalog_rabbitmqStep1Body: RabbitMQ.Client 7 and later emit OpenTelemetry spans themselves, so no separate instrumentation package is needed. Version 6 emits none.
dataSourceCatalog_rabbitmqStep2Heading: Listen to the client's activity sources
dataSourceCatalog_rabbitmqStep2Body: Add the RabbitMQ.Client activity sources to the tracer. Rows are named after the exchange you publish to. Messages sent through the default exchange appear under their queue name.
dataSourceCatalog_rabbitmqStep3Body: Queue depth isn't in spans. Run the OpenTelemetry Collector (contrib distribution) with the rabbitmq receiver. It reads the management API, so enable the rabbitmq_management plugin and create a user with the monitoring tag. The built-in guest user only works from localhost.
dataSourceCatalog_rabbitmqStep4Body: Publish and consume a few messages, then open Messaging in the top nav. Each exchange or queue appears within a few seconds; the backlog appears after one collection interval when a queue name matches the row or one of its routing keys.
dataSourceCatalog_customIntro: Flare.Ingest speaks plain OTLP - point any OTLP-capable exporter, collector, or HTTP client at it directly.
dataSourceCatalog_customStep2Body: Expect a 200 response with an empty body. The event is buffered for a couple seconds before it lands in ClickHouse, so give Logs a moment before checking.
dataSourceCatalog_customStep3Heading: If this deployment requires an ingest key
dataSourceCatalog_customStep3Body: Anonymous ingest is the default. If yours has been turned to required, create a key from an Admin session and send it as a Bearer token on every export.
